subject: psychiatry
title: Alcohol Withdrawal Syndromes and Delirium Tremens

steps.tx: **Alcohol withdrawal seizures**, historically termed rum fits, occur characteristically 12 to 48 hours after the reduction or cessation of heavy drinking. Seizures present as generalized tonic-clonic convulsions, often occurring in brief flurries of two to three seizures without focal features or post-ictal focal deficits.
steps.say: Withdrawal seizures occur twelve to forty-eight hours after stopping alcohol as non-focal generalized tonic-clonic convulsions in brief flurries.

vis.alt: Neuroadaptation and central neurotransmitter imbalance during acute substance withdrawal
vis.caption: Neuroadaptation and central neurotransmitter imbalance during acute substance withdrawal.

steps.tx: **Clinical progression of withdrawal states** follows a predictable chronobiological timeline: tremulousness begins at 6 to 8 hours, withdrawal seizures occur between 12 and 48 hours, alcoholic hallucinosis appears at 12 to 24 hours, and delirium tremens peaks at 72 to 96 hours post-cessation.
steps.say: Alcohol withdrawal follows a strict timeline: tremors at six hours, seizures at twenty-four hours, hallucinosis at twelve hours, and delirium tremens at three days.

vis.title: Chronology of Alcohol Withdrawal
rows: Fine tremor, sweating, tachycardia, mild anxiety
Brief cluster of generalized tonic-clonic seizures
Fluctuating consciousness, lilliputian visions, autonomic collapse

steps.tx: Read this timeline from the last drink on the left toward the later days on the right. Tremor, sweating, and anxiety appear first, followed in some patients by **withdrawal seizures** within two days. The dangerous end of the scale, delirium tremens, usually arrives after two to three days with confusion, hallucinations, and severe autonomic overactivity that can kill without prompt benzodiazepine treatment and monitoring.
steps.say: Withdrawal starts with tremor and anxiety, may bring seizures within two days, and can end in delirium tremens. That later stage is the life-threatening one.

vis.alt: Timeline of alcohol withdrawal from early tremulousness through withdrawal seizures to delirium tremens over the days after stopping drinking
vis.caption: Timeline of alcohol withdrawal syndromes, from tremulousness and withdrawal seizures through to delirium tremens. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: **Delirium tremens** is a medical emergency representing the most severe, life-threatening form of alcohol withdrawal, carrying a mortality rate up to 15 percent if untreated. Onset peaks between 72 and 96 hours after the last drink, characterized by fluctuating clouding of consciousness, severe confusion, autonomic hyperactivity, and agitation.
steps.say: Delirium tremens peaks three to four days after cessation, manifesting with clouded consciousness, autonomic instability, and vivid hallucinations.

left.title: Delirium Tremens
points: Disorientation to time, place, and person

right.title: Alcoholic Hallucinosis
points: Oriented to time, place, and person
Stable vital signs without autonomic storm

steps.tx: **Visual hallucinations in delirium tremens** are characteristically vivid, terrifying, and lilliputian in nature, featuring swarms of small insects, snakes, or diminutive people crawling over bedsheets or skin. Patients exhibit profound motor agitation, attempting to brush imaginary vermin from their bodies while completely disoriented to surroundings.
steps.say: Delirium tremens hallucinations are vivid and lilliputian, featuring small crawling insects or snakes that patients frantically try to brush away.

steps.tx: **Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol**, revised scale abbreviated CIWA-Ar, is the gold standard 10-item instrument for quantifying withdrawal severity and titrating treatment. Scoring evaluates nausea, tremor, paroxysmal sweats, anxiety, agitation, headache, and sensory disturbances; scores above 15 indicate severe withdrawal.
steps.say: The CIWA-Ar scale scores withdrawal severity from zero to sixty-seven across ten domains. Scores above fifteen require intensive pharmacotherapy.

vis.title: CIWA-Ar Severity Strata
rows: Supportive care, hydration, oral vitamins, no sedatives needed
Intensive inpatient monitoring; scheduled plus PRN benzodiazepines
High-dose intravenous benzodiazepines in intensive care unit

steps.tx: **Chlordiazepoxide** is the long-acting benzodiazepine of choice for managing alcohol withdrawal in patients with preserved hepatic function. Its long elimination half-life and active metabolites provide smooth, auto-tapering protection against rebound seizures and delirium tremens, administered as 50 to 100 milligrams every six hours.
steps.say: Chlordiazepoxide is the drug of choice for alcohol withdrawal due to its long half-life, providing auto-tapering protection against seizures.

left.title: Chlordiazepoxide (Long-Acting)
points: Elimination half-life up to one hundred hours
Preferred in patients with healthy liver function
Given orally in structured tapering schedules

right.title: Lorazepam (Intermediate-Acting)
points: Drug of choice in hepatic cirrhosis or failure
Available in intravenous and intramuscular forms
Safer in elderly and respiratory-compromised patients

steps.tx: **Lorazepam in hepatic impairment** represents the mandatory alternative benzodiazepine when managing alcohol withdrawal in patients with known cirrhosis, alcoholic hepatitis, or elevated transaminases. Because lorazepam undergoes simple Phase II glucuronidation without Phase I hepatic CYP metabolism, it does not accumulate dangerously or precipitate hepatic encephalopathy.
steps.say: Lorazepam is mandatory in liver disease because it relies on simple glucuronidation, avoiding dangerous drug accumulation or hepatic encephalopathy.

vis.title: Benzodiazepine Hepatic Selection
rows: Preferred drug of choice in cirrhosis

steps.tx: **Intravenous thiamine administration** must always precede any glucose infusion in patients undergoing alcohol withdrawal to prevent precipitating acute Wernicke encephalopathy. Thiamine functions as an essential pyrophosphate cofactor for pyruvate dehydrogenase and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase; glucose administration without thiamine triggers catastrophic thalamic and mammillary body necrosis.
steps.say: Intravenous thiamine must always precede glucose infusions to prevent acute Wernicke encephalopathy and irreversible mammillary body necrosis.

nodes.label: Exhausted thiamine stores in chronic alcohol dependence
Administer high-dose parenteral thiamine (minimum 200-500 mg IV)
Restore transketolase and pyruvate dehydrogenase enzymatic activity
Safe to initiate intravenous glucose and nutritional repletion
